title: The donoteat style
lede: What a donoteat01 video is made of, with links to the storyboard panels where each habit shows up.

sections.heading: How an episode is put together
sections.intro: Most videos follow the same order. A Cities: Skylines build plays on screen for nearly the whole runtime while the narration gives a history or policy lecture over it. The build illustrates the argument, and the game's cheerful feedback often argues against it.

items.name: Political preamble
items.text: Some Franklin episodes open with a statement about current events before the episode starts. Episode 4 opens with Abolish ICE and episode 7 with prison-strike solidarity. Episode 5 begins with a mock non-apology that ends on ABOLISH ICE filling the screen.

examples.note: A non-apology ends with ABOLISH ICE filling the screen.

items.name: Title over Beethoven
items.text: Franklin title sequences play the fourth movement of Beethoven's Fifth, in a high school orchestra recording.

items.name: The game as a foil
items.text: Tutorial moves and positive UI feedback are played straight and then set against what the game leaves out. Green smiles hover over a garage that replaced homes, and highway connections arrive before any people or history do.

examples.note: Highway connections arrive before any people or history do.
Cheerful park indicators ignore the narrator's questions about displaced residents.
Green smiles celebrate the garage next to a tally of destroyed homes.
The tutorial finishes polishing the parking whose costs it has just exposed.
A chorus of unhappy game faces reverses the opening everyone-wins premise.

items.name: The imaginary slide lecture
items.text: He asks an unseen grad student for the projector. A photo of a carousel projector appears, and the slides that follow arrive blurred, snap into focus and change with a mechanical clunk. In Public Housing Part 1 the operator loads a slide upside down.

examples.note: A Kodak Carousel photograph is presented as required equipment for architectural expertise.
Projector noise plays as the Urban Planning 101 slide comes into focus.
A carousel-projector photograph and projector sound open the architecture lecture.
The request to the imaginary grad student gets a literal equipment insert.
The operator puts a slide in upside down and the presenter asks for it to be flipped.
A literal projector image marks the switch into a classroom lecture.

items.name: "That's another episode"
items.text: Tangents are parked with a promise of a future episode, sometimes a specific one: a whole episode on sewers, Red Vienna deserving its own episode, a video to be called "Paul Joseph Watson doesn't understand architecture." An on-screen card in Gentrification points out that "later" means another episode.

examples.note: "Sewers are going to be an entirely different episode, by the way."
Capitalism can alter the weather, "but that's another episode."
New luxury buildings "might not last 20 years, but that's another episode."
Philadelphia's weak historic-preservation laws are "another episode."
A dry correction notes that 'later' means another episode, not later in this one.
Georgism: "that could be its own episode eventually."
"Eventually I'll do a video called, I don't know... Paul Joseph Watson doesn't understand architecture."
"Red Vienna probably deserves its own episode at some point."
The old Penn Station, "that maybe we'll talk about in a later video."
Prison-like radial high schools: "another topic for another day."

items.name: The commercial
items.text: Near the end he announces the switch, as in "Okay, so that was the episode. Here's the commercial." The pitch then works against itself. Coffee money will be spent on beer, you are welcome to pirate the bonus episode, and at $15 an hour, four minutes spent hunting for a pirated copy costs more than the dollar. Because the channel runs no ads, Dennis Prager does not appear before the video.

items.name: Merch and the patron rivalry
items.text: The commercial also sells imaginary merchandise, such as a BORN TO RAZE shirt for highway demolition, and charts the channel's patron count as a rivalry with Jordan Peterson, complete with lobsters and a red LOL arrow.

items.name: Cinematics and credits
items.text: After the commercial come patron credits and a cinematic of the finished build without the game UI. Public-domain recordings of Mendelssohn, Beethoven or Grieg play underneath. Episode 5 uses classical music to keep its promise of no techno.

examples.note: Beethoven's Fifth, III, accompanies the closing cinematic reveal.
Mendelssohn's The Hebrides plays under the UI-free aerial reveal.
Grieg's 'Aase's Death' accompanies the closing cinematic.
Classical music fulfils the opening promise of no techno in the cinematics.
The Hebrides opens the cinematics.

items.name: The fare token
items.text: Videos end with a DNE token reading GOOD FOR ONE FARE, which drops out of frame to leave black. Urban Freeways uses the token for a fake ending at 1:14, then returns to gameplay for another 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Narration
sections.intro: Viewers have compared the voice to a retiree or contractor patiently explaining why your home addition will cost ten times as much and take three times as long. The delivery stays level for statistics and punchlines alike, so a joke arrives in the same tone as the history around it.

items.name: Verbal habits
items.text: Across the 24 transcripts, he tags "right?" onto claims 204 times in 13 videos and says "folks" 85 times in 19, as in "Protectionism. It works, folks." "Anyway" (57 times in 20 videos) is how he leaves a tangent. In Banking & Commerce he checks in mid-explanation: "Are you following this? Okay, good."

items.name: The ANYWAY card
items.text: After an outrageous satirical tangent, a black card reading ANYWAY moves on as if nothing happened.

items.name: "Crony capitalism is just capitalism"
items.text: He says the line in TRAINS! and again in the Budd video, where a caption adds IS JUST CAPITALISM under CRONY CAPITALISM. Organized Labor rejects the label on screen the same way.

examples.note: IS JUST CAPITALISM is added after CRONY CAPITALISM.

items.name: Fake partisanship
items.text: "As a red-blooded American, I just want to say this. I hate liberals." The collage that follows puts conservatives among the liberals, and the episode later sorts Reagan, Obama and Trump under the same label.

items.name: Mock-documentary tall tales
items.text: An invented first-person story or a satirical position gets date cards, maps, redaction bars and sober archival photos. The story escalates, or the photographs contradict what he is saying. Episode 4's trip to Cambodia and Organized Labor's Hoffa story both work this way.

examples.note: A mock-censorship bar hides the university credential for an implausible 1976 trip.
Children with empty bowls undercut the narrated praise for abolishing currency.
Shelves of skulls contradict the claim that minorities were treated with compassion.
A redaction bar gives the fabricated Hoffa adventure mock-clandestine credibility.
The fabricated Hoffa itinerary gains absurd geographic detail when it moves to Argentina.
The invented Hoffa story ends with an anti-Reagan punchline over a sober photograph.

items.name: Mispronunciation
items.text: French names and terms are mangled on purpose, often enough that the series eventually asks itself why there is so much French. "Bourgeois" gets its own spelling and pronunciation joke.

sections.heading: Visual jokes
sections.intro: Most visual gags are single inserts that last a second or two between gameplay shots, and they are easy to miss at normal speed.

items.name: Puns made literal
items.text: A term is said aloud and the edit cuts to a picture of the thing it sounds like. Ottoman repairs get a footstool, and the sin tax becomes a syntax-error popup.

examples.note: Repairs by the Ottoman Empire are illustrated with a piece of ottoman furniture.
'Multiple purposes' becomes two marine mammals, multiple porpoises.
The shipping term staple port is answered with a red office stapler.
The Kraft pulping process becomes a box of Kraft mac and cheese.
A computer syntax-error popup turns the spoken 'sin tax' into a visual pun.
A duck appears under LESS DUCTILITY.
Jackson's pet banks become a literal pet kitten.
FUD (fear, uncertainty and doubt) is illustrated with Elmer Fudd.

items.name: The wrong person
items.text: A name or acronym brings up the wrong referent first. Alexander Hamilton becomes the F1 driver Lewis Hamilton. Saying Sargon of Akkad brings up Paul Joseph Watson, and the narrator says "No, not that guy."

examples.note: Engineer Marc Brunel's name brings up NFL quarterback Mark Brunell.
Alexander Hamilton is swapped for the F1 driver Lewis Hamilton.
The National Bar Association gets the basketball league's NBA logo.
Saying 'Sargon of Akkad' first brings up Paul Joseph Watson, and the narrator says 'No, not that guy.'
The place name Bowie triggers an insert of the musician.
The structural 'buff test' is illustrated with Arnold Schwarzenegger.
Blast-furnace coke is first shown as a can of Coca-Cola.
The Resettlement Administration's acronym RA turns into masked gunmen, the 'other RA'.

items.name: Cartoons at the end of a serious list
items.text: A montage of documentary images ends on a SpongeBob, Futurama or Thomas & Friends character. Squidward stands in for retail workers and Scruffy for janitors.

examples.note: A sober prison-labor list ends on SpongeBob in a call-center headset.
Squidward the cashier stands in for retail workers in the essential-labor montage.
Futurama's Scruffy closes the occupation montage for janitors.
Squidward starts a SpongeBob corporate hierarchy for upper management.
Patrick's rock stands in for the poor relocation options offered to tenants.
Futurama's Nixon is the face of the halt to public-housing construction.
Futurama's Bender illustrates ductility.
Thomas the Tank Engine illustrates the serious railroads-and-transit agenda item.

items.name: Other games
items.text: Processes are acted out in other games, usually Minecraft. Water supply is carrying a bucket, and a house fire keeps burning in the background of the Budd video's metallurgy lecture. Europa Universalis IV and SimCity 2000 also turn up.

examples.note: Municipal water supply is shown as carrying a bucket in Minecraft.
Minecraft mining illustrates nineteenth-century explosive tunneling.
The Minecraft house fire behind the metallurgy lecture reaches its floating-inferno payoff.
The generic factory is a crude block-built Minecraft workshop.
The DRAW PAY HERE station hands over a meagre ingot wage.
A demand for conquest footage gets a screenshot of Europa Universalis IV instead.
The SimCity 2000 arcology menu stands in for extravagant city-building fantasy.

items.name: Type that keeps growing
items.text: A demand repeats in bigger lettering until it overflows the frame. Rent control is the usual subject, and the Loop video answers the gadget pitches with BUILD A FUCKING TRAIN.

examples.note: The correction card breaks into fragmented giant words on its third repetition.
The rent-control recommendation grows too large to fit on screen.
The rent-control card returns cropped even tighter.
A non-apology ends with ABOLISH ICE filling the screen.
A giant BUILD A FUCKING TRAIN card answers the gadget sales pitches.
WORLD DOMINATION appears in huge type to pay off the organizing refrain.
A proposed rent-control shirt slogan becomes an emphatic standalone graphic.

items.name: Scare quotes
items.text: An official's or developer's euphemism goes on a plain card in quotation marks, and the narration translates it: "ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT" means a handout, "RESTORED ORDER" means arresting the victims.

examples.note: FIX TRAFFIC appears in sarcastic quotation marks.
Scare quotes turn EFFICIENCY into a punchline about profitability.
The scare-quoted ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT card is decoded as a handout to developers and institutions.
In RESTORED ORDER, the scare quotes expose that order was restored by arresting the victims.
APOLITICAL in scare quotes questions business unions' claimed neutrality.
Scare quotes around 'apprentice' undermine the promise of education.
Heemeyer's ILLEGAL REZONING complaint appears in scare quotes, and the narration undercuts it.

items.name: The editor talks back
items.text: On-screen text corrects or overrules the narrator. A pedantic Wikipedia page fixes the colony's country to Denmark–Norway, and an overlay corrects his 178 mph to 183.

examples.note: A parenthetical card corrects the speaker's pre-Magna Carta dating to 1663.
A terse Queen Village card sidesteps the debate over pronouncing Southwark.
A *183 MPH overlay corrects the spoken 178 mph.
A pedantic Wikipedia page corrects the colony's country to Denmark–Norway.
A caption admits that the illustrated 'rifles' are muskets.
An on-screen correction reverses the complaint: mail does go by train and plane.
A dry correction notes that 'later' means another episode, not later in this one.
IS JUST CAPITALISM is added after CRONY CAPITALISM.

sections.heading: Sound
sections.intro: Recognizable stings and anthems land punchlines without needing a picture.

items.name: Stings
items.text: Every time he says "law and order" in Law & Order, the TV show's DUN-DUN plays. He asks whether it will do this every time and later dodges the phrase with "law and... uh, imprisonment." When the sign-off "that was the Law and Order episode" sets it off one last time, he grunts before finishing the sentence. Elsewhere a Wilhelm scream follows "the Spanish," a sad trombone accompanies Henry stuck in his tunnel, and an audience boos the SOCIAL DEMOCRATS card.

examples.note: The Law & Order DUN-DUN sting answers the phrase 'law and order.'
The sign-off "that was the Law and Order episode" sets off the sting, and he grunts "urgh" before "episode."
A Wilhelm scream follows 'the Spanish.'
A sad trombone punctuates Henry being stuck in a tunnel.
An audience-booing effect greets the SOCIAL DEMOCRATS card.

items.name: Anthems and found music
items.text: "March of the Volunteers" turns road-building into patriotic service to the Chinese state. The promised soothing footage for the LIHTC explanation is a North Korean military parade, and "Let's All Go to the Lobby" plays over a premiere intermission.

examples.note: March of the Volunteers turns road-building into patriotic service to the Chinese state.
The North Korean anthem plays under the promised 'soothing' LIHTC explanation.
'Let's All Go to the Lobby' plays over the premiere intermission.

sections.heading: Running gags across videos
sections.intro: These turn up in more than one video.

items.name: The sunglasses sun
items.text: A cartoon sun in sunglasses smiles over deliberately crude engineering diagrams.

items.name: The poop emoji
items.text: Any mention of sewage brings up a giant cheerful poop emoji or a POOP label.

items.name: The "unrelated" gunmen
items.text: Acronyms like RA and IRA, or a mention of Catholics, cut to masked armed men, sometimes labeled "unrelated" or followed by "Tiocfaidh ár lá."

items.name: Rich Uncle Pennybags
items.text: The Monopoly man or a generic top-hatted caricature stands in for capitalists and landlords.

items.name: Saxophone Clinton
items.text: Bill Clinton appears playing the saxophone where a policy image would go.

items.name: Bodybuilder Bernie
items.text: A hugely muscular Bernie Sanders announces the left opposition.

items.name: Scruffy the janitor
items.text: Futurama's reclining janitor stands in for maintenance labor.

items.name: Henry in the tunnel
items.text: Henry from Thomas & Friends, walled up in a tunnel, stands for failed steam machinery.

items.name: Rent control
items.text: Rent control keeps coming back as the answer, in ever larger type and once as a shirt slogan.

items.name: The Chinese anthem
items.text: "March of the Volunteers" plays under jokes about state-socialist shortcuts.

items.name: InfoWars
items.text: Absurd claims get sent to InfoWars.

items.name: Sargon of Akkad
items.text: The ancient king keeps getting confused with Carl Benjamin's YouTube persona.

items.name: Hyperloop and Lyle Lanley
items.text: Hyperloop and the Simpsons monorail salesman stand in for transit hype.

items.name: Redacted credentials
items.text: A made-up personal history gets a mock-censorship bar.

items.name: Combat Liberalism
items.text: Mao's Combat Liberalism is reused or retitled as a literal visual.

items.name: Killdozer
items.text: Floated as a bonus-episode topic, promoted in commercials, then delivered.

items.name: Content warnings on the CW
items.text: A content warning is literalized as the CW television network.

sections.intro: Many videos build a joke early and pay it off later in the same video.
